Two positions can be distinguished: On the one hand, both psychotherapy and placebo are psychologic interventions with proven clinically significant effects and similar mechanisms. But on the other hand, they are perceived as rather different - if not opposite - in both appearance as well as true nature. This review presents a historical perspective on the shared genesis of placebo and psychotherapy, touches upon the importance of how placebo and psychotherapy are defined, discusses the designs and uses of placebo-control conditions in psychotherapy research, examines the possibility of placebo psychotherapy, and considers how the appreciation of the respective finding depends on the underlying definition of psychotherapy. It is concluded that psychotherapy and placebo might share more than readily apparent or considered acceptable but that the appreciation of what is usually seen as clinical chaff might not only be feasible but also warranted.

screening.rationale: Narrative review focused explicitly on the relationship between placebo and psychotherapy (history, definitions, placebo-control designs), so placebo is the main subject.

classification.summary: Reviewed historical and conceptual relations between psychotherapy and placebo, definitions, control designs, and implications for psychotherapy research.

title: Open-label nondeceptive placebos.
abstract: Open-label placebos (OLPs), where patients are informed they are receiving a placebo, challenge the traditional notion that placebos require deception to be effective. Recent research has shown that OLPs can positively impact subjective outcomes, such as pain perception and symptom severity, across various conditions like chronic pain, mental disorders, and other symptoms. However, their efficacy varies depending on the condition and duration of treatment. In placebo analgesia, neurobiologic studies suggest that OLPs activate brain pathways involved in pain relief, indicating shared mechanisms with traditional placebos. Despite these findings, the exact mechanisms driving OLP efficacy remain unclear, highlighting the need for further research. In the past, concerns about the robustness of OLP studies, potential biases, and results' generalizability have risen. Ensuring transparency and balancing participant engagement across study groups are crucial to addressing these concerns. In clinical practice, OLPs have shown promise, particularly in reducing medication doses while maintaining therapeutic benefits, such as postoperative pain management. This suggests that OLPs provide a nondeceptive alternative in cases where conventional treatments are ineffective or have undesirable side-effects. Future research should focus on large-scale, rigorously designed trials to confirm the efficacy of OLPs and further explore their underlying mechanisms. As a nondeceptive approach, OLPs offer a relevant ethical advancement in placebo research, with the potential to improve patient care in specific clinical settings.

screening.rationale: Review focused explicitly on open-label placebos, their efficacy, mechanisms, and clinical implications, making placebo phenomena the paper's primary subject.

classification.summary: Reviewed evidence on open-label placebos, concluding they can improve subjective outcomes (e.g., pain, symptoms) and engage brain pain pathways, but efficacy varied and more rigorous trials are needed.
classification.key_finding: Found that open-label placebos produced subjective symptom improvements and activated neural pain-related circuits, though effects were heterogeneous across conditions and study quality.

title: Hypoxia.
abstract: Placebo and nocebo effects are particularly relevant in hypoxia research. Studies performed at high-altitude environments have shown that placebos can partially mimic the effects of oxygen (O2) and compensate for some of the imbalances at the level of critical life functions, such as ventilation, circulation, and even performance. In contrast, nocebos can exacerbate symptoms of hypoxia, suggesting how the brain can influence physiology even in conditions in which survival is at stake. Knowledge from research on placebo and nocebo effects at high altitudes may be incorporated into the treatment of respiratory diseases, for which psychologic aspects are no less important than physiological factors. Indeed, there is evidence that beliefs and expectations can influence responses to O2 deprivation in patients with respiratory diseases. Acknowledging the role of placebos and nocebos in natural hypoxic conditions can translate into a better management of hypoxic patients in medical settings and offer an opportunity to optimize O2 utilization strategies and enhance symptom management.

screening.rationale: Narrative review explicitly discusses placebo and nocebo effects in hypoxia, summarizing evidence and implications, so placebo/nocebo is a substantive topic within the paper.

classification.summary: Reviews evidence that placebo and nocebo effects influence physiological and symptomatic responses to hypoxia and high-altitude exposure, and discusses implications for respiratory disease management.

title: Minimizing placebo responses in clinical trials.
abstract: Over the past decades, a growing number of clinical trials in neurologic conditions have failed to demonstrate superiority of active treatments over placebo. A key question in this context is whether an increase in placebo response can explain these trial failures, potentially hindering the development and approval of new therapies. Within this discussion, an underlying assumption appears to be that it is both feasible and beneficial to minimize the placebo responses in clinical trials and thereby improve the drug-placebo ratio. This chapter explores the predominant suggestions occurring in the literature on our opportunities to minimize placebo responses in clinical trials and evaluates the supporting evidence. Furthermore, we discuss whether reducing placebo responses necessarily enhances drug responses and promote successful trials. Finally, we propose leveraging insights from placebo mechanism research to refine RCT methodologies, for example, by incorporating patients' perceptions, emotional feelings, and expectations toward treatments and treatment effects. This approach may yield more ecologically valid trial outcomes for both pharmacological and nonpharmacological treatments in neurologic conditions.

screening.rationale: Included because this is a review whose explicit focus is placebo responses in clinical trials and on methods to minimize/placebo-related effects (placebo science and trial methodology).

classification.summary: Reviews literature on minimizing placebo responses in neurologic RCTs, evaluated supporting evidence, and discussed implications for trial design and leveraging placebo mechanisms.

title: Placebo effects in mental disorders.
abstract: This chapter delves into the multifaceted role of placebo effects in mental disorders, highlighting their impact on treatment outcomes across a spectrum of conditions, including depression, anxiety, schizophrenia, and bipolar disorder. Placebo responses, often seen as the intersection of psychological and physiological healing mechanisms, are critically examined through systematic reviews and meta-analyses that compare placebo effects to active treatments. The findings underscore substantial placebo effects, particularly in depression and anxiety, where these effects are often comparable to those of pharmacological interventions. The chapter also explores the variability of placebo effects across different disorders and the implications for clinical practice, suggesting that understanding these effects could lead to more tailored and effective therapeutic approaches. Additionally, the discussion includes the potential of open-label placebos, the influence of patient expectations, and the role of the clinician-patient relationship in enhancing treatment outcomes. By dissecting these elements, the chapter aims to pave the way for integrating placebo mechanisms into clinical practice, thereby enhancing the overall effectiveness of mental health treatments.

screening.rationale: Chapter explicitly reviews placebo effects and responses in mental disorders, summarizing systematic reviews and meta-analyses, so placebo phenomena are the paper's primary subject (inclusion rule 4).

classification.summary: Reviews evidence on placebo effects and placebo responses across mental disorders, highlighting substantial placebo effects in depression and anxiety and discussing mechanisms such as expectations, clinician interaction, and open-label placebos.
classification.key_finding: Found that placebo responses are often substantial in depression and anxiety and can approach pharmacological effect sizes; discusses mechanisms and clinical implications.

title: Placebo and the doctor-patient interaction and communication.
abstract: A main pathway of placebo and nocebo effects occurs via communication in patient-provider interactions. It is therefore of crucial importance to get insight into how positive or (unintendedly) negative expectancies about treatments are induced during healthcare provider-patient interaction and how possible undesired and unnecessary treatment outcomes can be altered. In this chapter, we outline the theoretical background of placebo effects and patient-provider interactions from the perspective of medical communication and placebo research as well as the functions of medical communication. We subsequently summarize the evidence on patient-provider interactions that alter placebo and nocebo effects, with a specific focus on the existing evidence in neurologic disorders. Specifically, we focus on different phases of patient-provider interactions during the consultations, such as outline of the treatment rationale, doses and efficacy of treatments, medical procedures as well as side-effects and risks. Eventually, the chapters focuses on possibilities for education and training of patient-provider interactions to increase knowledge, create awareness, and practice skills of optimizing placebo effects and minimizing nocebo effects during patient-provider interactions, by making use of advanced technological developments, such as Virtual Reality.

screening.rationale: Review chapter focused explicitly on how patient–provider communication induces and alters placebo and nocebo effects, summarizing evidence and interventions in neurology.

classification.summary: Reviewed theory and evidence on how patient–provider communication generates placebo and nocebo effects, focusing on neurologic disorders and training/technological approaches to optimize outcomes.

title: The COVID-19 pandemic: a special case of placebo and nocebo effects.
abstract: In late 2019, reports of pneumonia from an unknown cause marked the beginning of an unprecedented health crisis with far-reaching societal consequences. The ensuing global pandemic placed immense strain on healthcare systems, disrupted economies, and altered the way that we work, communicate, and interact. Importantly, as the SARS-Cov-2 (COVID-19) virus spread, so did a range of psychological stressors, including fear, anxiety, and uncertainty. This chapter examines the trajectory of placebo- and nocebo-relevant factors during the early, mid, and late stages of the pandemic, highlighting their impact on health outcomes and human behavior. Understanding the interplay between psychological and physical health during the pandemic is crucial for minimizing maladaptive health outcomes in the future. We therefore review current strategies for mitigating the nocebo effect and leveraging the placebo effect that may be employed to enhance health and well-being and attenuate pandemic-related harms.

screening.rationale: Narrative review explicitly focused on placebo- and nocebo-relevant factors during the COVID-19 pandemic and on strategies to mitigate nocebo and leverage placebo effects (review of placebo/nocebo phenomena).

classification.summary: Reviews placebo- and nocebo-relevant factors across the COVID-19 pandemic and summarizes strategies to mitigate nocebo effects and harness placebo effects to protect health.

title: Peripheral neuropathies.
abstract: The present chapter is an overview of peripheral neuropathies for which placebo and nocebo responses and/or placebo and nocebo effects have been investigated to date. Even if most of our knowledge in this field comes from pain studies, a rapidly expanding picture emerges from the original research works conducted over the past 7 years on: painful diabetic neuropathy, postherpetic neuralgia, neuropathic complications of thoracotomy, carpal tunnel syndrome, Guillain-Barré syndrome, and chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIPD). Otherwise, very little, if anything, is known for the other peripheral neuropathies. Significant placebo effects were reported for neuropathic complications of thoracotomy and CIPD. Treatment expectations emerged as predictors of treatment outcome in neuropathic complications of thoracotomy. Finally, special attention to contextual factors, inclusion of no treatment arms, and control for baseline covariates should be given to further improve research in clinical trials of peripheral neuropathy.

screening.rationale: The chapter is an explicit review of placebo and nocebo responses/effects in peripheral neuropathies (stated aim and synthesis of findings).

classification.summary: Reviews placebo and nocebo effects and responses reported in peripheral neuropathies, highlighting significant placebo effects in thoracotomy-related neuropathy and CIDP and the role of treatment expectations as predictors.
classification.key_finding: Found significant placebo effects for neuropathic complications of thoracotomy and CIDP, and that treatment expectations predicted outcomes in thoracotomy neuropathy.

title: The motor system and motor disorders.
abstract: The beneficial effects of placebos and the harmful effects of nocebos on motor functions concern not only sports performance but also pathological conditions and, in particular, movement disorders. In the pathological context, most studies have been conducted on Parkinson disease, where placebo and nocebo can influence motor and nonmotor symptoms, modulate the activity of subcortical and cortical brain regions, and, in the case of placebos, induce the dopaminergic release in the basal ganglia. In contrast, knowledge about placebo and nocebo effects in other movement disorders is still limited and derives mainly from randomized control studies in which the term "placebo response" is more appropriate than "placebo effect." As will be illustrated in this chapter, the study of placebo and nocebo effects in the motor domain has addressed different motor functions involving more focused body districts or the entire body and has allowed discovering the involvement of a set of cortical and subcortical brain structures belonging to the motor control network.

screening.rationale: The chapter is a review whose explicit subject is placebo and nocebo effects on motor function (Parkinson's and sports), meeting inclusion criterion for reviews of placebo/nocebo.

classification.summary: Reviews placebo and nocebo effects on motor functions, focusing on Parkinson disease, sports performance, and dopaminergic and neural-circuit mechanisms.
classification.key_finding: Reports that placebo administration can induce dopaminergic release in basal ganglia and that evidence beyond Parkinson disease is limited.

title: The placebome.
abstract: Placebos in randomized clinical trials (RCTs) control for many nonspecific factors that influence clinical outcomes, beyond the active agent being tested. These include the "placebo effect," regression to the mean, clinician bias, Hawthorne effects, and the natural history of the condition or disease. The impact of these factors together constitute the "placebo response." A key assumption in RCTs is that the placebo response is a discrete component of response to drug, and thus placebo and drug responses are additive. Based on this additivity assumption, the efficacy of a drug is generally determined to be the difference between the drug and placebo responses. There is evidence that genetic variation can influence at least two key components of placebo response in RCTs: placebo effects and the natural history of the disease process. Further, although some drugs, like naloxone, can modify placebo effects, little is known about the potential for genetic variation to modify the effects of these drugs relative to placebo. If genetic influences on patients vary between the drug and placebo arm, potential gene-by-drug/placebo interactions could mask treatment effects. Here, we review evidence that genetic variation in the placebome - the group of genome-related mediators that affect an individual's response to placebo treatments - could confound results of RCTs through differential effects in the drug and placebo treatment arms.

screening.rationale: Review focused on genetic moderators of placebo effects/placebo response (the 'placebome'), making placebo response the explicit subject.

classification.summary: Reviews evidence that genetic variation (the 'placebome') influences placebo effects and could differentially affect drug and placebo arms in RCTs, potentially confounding trial results.
classification.key_finding: Argued that gene-by-drug/placebo interactions may mask or alter apparent drug efficacy in randomized trials.

title: Conditioned immune responses and the neural-immune connection in animals and humans.
abstract: Continuous drug treatment is essential for managing immune-related clinical conditions. However, the significant adverse side-effects associated with immunosuppressive drugs call for alternative or complementary treatment approaches. In experimental animals, as well as in healthy individuals and patient populations, controlled drug-dose reduction has been shown to be achievable via taste-immune associative learning paradigms without compromising efficacy of treatment. A systematic use of such conditioned immunopharmacological responses may therefore be considered as a supportive treatment tool in clinical settings to optimize patients' outcomes. This chapter provides an overview of the neural-immune connection in animals and humans and discusses approaches, translational aspects, and the applicability of learning paradigms in clinical settings.

screening.rationale: Narrative review focused on conditioned immunopharmacological responses and neural-immune mechanisms, meeting inclusion as a placebo-science review of classical conditioning mechanisms (rule 4/3).

classification.summary: Reviews conditioned immunopharmacological responses in animals and humans and discussed neural-immune mechanisms and translational applications of associative learning to reduce drug dosing.

title: A brief history of placebo.
abstract: History of medicine is the history of placebo. Over the course of several centuries, treatments with a physical and spiritual approach were the rule. Clinical trials have become the gold standard to test the efficacy of new treatments only over the past few decades. We have learned that the placebo response, that is, the global response to a placebo, consists of many factors: one of them is the placebo effect, that is, the real psychobiological phenomenon. Other factors include, but are not limited to, spontaneous remission, regression to the mean, unidentified covariables, and background noise. There is not a single placebo effect but many, and the different placebo effects are associated with demonstrable brain changes and the modification of endogenous chemicals in a way that may share similar mechanisms with pharmacological agents. The major mediators of the placebo effects are expectations and conditioning. They are interrelated, affect each other and operate in animals and humans. The nocebo effect goes in the opposite direction, whereby negative expectations may lead to negative outcomes. This brief overview on the emergence of the concept of placebo helps us understand how modern research approaches placebo and nocebo from a psychological, biological and neuroscientific perspective.

screening.rationale: Narrative review whose explicit subject is the history and conceptualization of placebo and nocebo mechanisms (placebo science), meeting inclusion rule for reviews focused on placebo/nocebo.

classification.summary: Reviews the historical emergence and conceptualization of placebo and nocebo, emphasizing expectation, conditioning, and neuroscientific findings linking placebo effects to brain and endogenous chemical changes.

title: Ethical considerations with using placebo treatments and effects in clinical practice.
abstract: Placebo effects have garnered increasing attention in recent decades. Research has demonstrated the existence of neurobiologic and neuropsychologic mechanisms underlying these effects, suggesting their genuine psychobiological nature. Harnessing these mechanisms by increasing placebo and minimizing nocebo effects in clinical practice is not possible without careful ethical consideration. This chapter explores the ethical dimensions surrounding the use of placebo effects in healthcare. It examines two kinds of placebo interventions - first through the use of placebo treatments and second by enhancing contextual factors - and gives an overview of the ethical questions pertinent to clinicians for each approach. Emphasizing the importance of clinician training in medical ethics, the chapter advocates for integrating placebo and nocebo effect awareness into standard training curriculum and introduces the fundamental concepts that should be considered by educators and clinicians alike. By fostering a nuanced understanding of placebo effects and their ethical implications, healthcare providers could optimize care without compromising on ethical integrity. Such an approach could be viewed as the "icing on the cake" of an evidence-based patient-centered care.

screening.rationale: Chapter is a focused review of ethical issues in using placebo treatments and contextual enhancement in clinical practice, making placebo science its primary subject.

classification.summary: Reviews ethical issues and educational implications of using placebo treatments and enhancing contextual factors to harness placebo and minimize nocebo effects in clinical practice.

title: Miscellaneous neurologic conditions with a few or no available data.
abstract: In this chapter, we will review the available literature on the nature of the placebo effect in conditions that are not well studied in terms of their response to the placebo intervention such as fatigue in general and in the context of myasthenia gravis and chronic fatigue syndrome, insomnia, restless leg syndrome, and central conditions such as multiple sclerosis. The clinical trials are either small or lack a natural history arm or a real placebo arm, therefore no definitive conclusions can be drawn regarding the magnitude and possible mechanisms of the placebo effect in these conditions. In addition, we will review some studies in conditions other than neurology, such as cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary diseases that can be of some interest to neurologists. Overall, we know very little, if any, about the psychobiological underpinnings in these medical conditions, and this lack of knowledge must be the stimulus for the pursuit of new future research.

screening.rationale: Narrative review chapter whose explicit focus is reviewing the placebo effect across multiple understudied neurological and related conditions, matching inclusion criterion for reviews of placebo/nocebo.

classification.summary: Reviewed the literature on placebo effects in understudied neurological (and related medical) conditions, found little definitive evidence and highlighted major knowledge gaps and need for future research.

title: Age and gender.
abstract: The specific role of age in the placebo effect has only recently become a focus of systematic studies. Prior to our 2013 review, the literature on placebo effects in children and adolescents was sparse, leaving significant gaps in understanding. Since then, several reviews and meta-analyses have addressed placebo responses in pediatric clinical trials, alongside experimental studies, comparing placebo effects between children, adolescents, and adults. This chapter provides a comprehensive overview of the current knowledge in this domain. Contrary to earlier assumptions, evidence suggests that placebo effects are not systematically larger in children than in adults. Sex differences in placebo responses/effects appear sporadic rather than consistent. Psychological mechanisms underlying the placebo effect, such as expectancy, conditioning, and patient-practitioner interaction, are largely the same in children and adults, though their relative importance may differ across age groups. However, the neurobiologic underpinnings of placebo effects in children remain poorly understood, with existing research providing only preliminary insights. Despite these gaps, the mechanisms of the placebo effect can and should be harnessed to enhance therapeutic outcomes in pediatric clinical practice. Leveraging these mechanisms to maximize placebo responses, while simultaneously minimizing nocebo effects, holds significant potential for improving care in children and adolescents.

screening.rationale: Review chapter focused explicitly on placebo effects and responses across age and sex, synthesizing evidence and mechanisms (meets inclusion rule 4).

classification.summary: Reviews evidence on age and sex differences in placebo effects and underlying mechanisms, concluding no systematic larger placebo effects in children and inconsistent sex differences, and recommends leveraging placebo mechanisms in pediatric care.
classification.key_finding: Found that placebo effects are not systematically larger in children than adults and sex differences are sporadic rather than consistent.

title: Understanding the psychology of the nocebo effect.
abstract: The nocebo effect is increasingly recognized as a powerful determinant of negative health outcomes across a range of symptoms, diseases, and treatments. Like the placebo, nocebo effects are generated by factors surrounding the treatment context, rather than active ingredients of treatments themselves. This chapter first describes the wide range of conditions in which nocebo effects have been clinically and experimentally demonstrated, including, pain, side-effects, and gastrointestinal symptoms. We then discuss the nocebo effect as a learning phenomenon, highlighting the ways by which verbal, conditioned, and social cues are integrated to produce nocebo effects. The chapter then explores mechanisms from psychology and neurobiology implicated in translating this learning to nocebo effects, including expectancy, anxiety, attention, and dispositional factors. Finally, the chapter identifies three potential mitigation strategies, which show some promise in minimizing the clinical burden of the nocebo effect.

screening.rationale: Review chapter explicitly focused on the nocebo effect, its mechanisms, evidence across conditions, and mitigation strategies, meeting inclusion criterion for reviews of placebo/nocebo phenomena.

classification.summary: Reviewed evidence and theory on nocebo effects across symptoms and conditions, described learning- and neurobiological mechanisms, and discussed strategies to mitigate clinical nocebo harms.

title: Placebo effects and emotion regulation: conceptual and neural similarities and differences.
abstract: Placebo effects are a family of diverse effects that tap into the brain and body's latent endogenous therapeutic potential. Unlike placebo responses, which can reflect statistical artifacts and natural history, placebo effects are driven by multiple types of psychological and brain responses to the treatment context. These include memories and learned associations from past experiences, expectations about future outcomes, cognitive appraisals of the self and context, and emotional states arising from these. Likewise, these psychological and brain responses to placebo arise from multiple aspects of the therapeutic encounter, including the relationship with the care provider, specific treatment cues like procedures and setting, and suggestions. Thus, many forms of placebo effect depend on the thoughts and imagination of the patient, and their interaction with the social and physical elements of the treatment context. In this way, placebo effects may overlap with cognitive self-regulation, a family of techniques that involve using attention, appraisal, and imagination to influence one's emotions, pain, and motivation based on regulatory goals. In this chapter, we focus on the relationship between placebo effects and self-regulation of emotion. We review research on placebo effects, focusing on the idea that changes in brain processes related to affect and motivation are central and consistently identified across disorders. We then describe studies of the cognitive regulation of emotion and pain, highlighting several commonalities shared by self-regulation and placebo. The picture that is emerging is one in which appraisals of the treatment context - influenced by both placebo treatments and self-regulatory goals - shape brain systems involved in the construction of value, feelings, and motivation. These systems are central to clinical outcomes that depend on feelings and function, and interact with learning processes to alter therapeutic trajectories across disorders.

screening.rationale: Narrative review whose explicit focus is placebo effects and their neural/psychological mechanisms and relation to emotion regulation, meeting inclusion criterion for reviews of placebo.

classification.summary: Reviews neural and conceptual overlaps and differences between placebo effects and emotion regulation, emphasizing expectation, learning, appraisal, and treatment-context mechanisms across disorders.
classification.key_finding: Argues that appraisal and brain value/motivation systems mediate placebo effects and overlap with cognitive emotion-regulation processes.

title: The role of observational learning in the formation of placebo and nocebo effects.
abstract: Placebo and nocebo effects are learning phenomena that can be induced not only through direct experience (e.g., classical and operant conditioning) or information (e.g., verbal suggestions), but also through indirect experience via observational learning. Observational learning is not only a powerful method for inducing placebo and nocebo effects; it is also a key mechanism that explains how these effects are formed. This chapter summarizes evidence on the effectiveness of observational learning in inducing placebo and nocebo effects across various symptoms and conditions, including pain. The role of three different types of observational learning - behavioral, symbolic, and verbal modeling - in the induction of these effects is discussed. Furthermore, the chapter reviews the psychological mechanisms, such as expectations, and the neural mechanisms that underlie observationally induced placebo effects. Key factors influencing the effectiveness of observational learning are considered, including the characteristics of both the model (e.g., sex, social status, self-confidence, and accuracy) and the observer (e.g., trait empathy). To provide an overview of the current understanding, the social learning model of placebo effects is introduced. Finally, directions for future research and the clinical implications of studies on observational learning in placebo and nocebo effects are explored.

screening.rationale: Review chapter explicitly focused on observational learning as a mechanism producing placebo and nocebo effects, meeting criterion 4 for inclusion.

classification.summary: Reviews evidence that observational learning (behavioral, symbolic, verbal modeling) can induce placebo and nocebo effects across symptoms including pain, and summarized psychological, neural mechanisms and key moderators.

title: Interventional procedures and physical therapies.
abstract: Placebo effects are inherent in all healthcare encounters and are underpinned by the therapeutic context. Every therapeutic context is rich in its ability to initiate and maintain placebo mechanisms, with the healthcare provider clinician interaction a crucial cornerstone. When one adds the powerful elements of touch, such as in physical therapies, and the technology and ritual associated with percutaneous or surgical interventions, robust placebo effects can be generated. However, the very elements of the therapeutic context and ritual that come with touch and intervention provide challenges. For those who design clinical trials, the ability to have an adequate placebo control maintaining robust blinding remains problematic as is the broader role of using placebo groups over other forms of controls. Nevertheless, researchers, clinicians, and patients need to better understand the relative contribution of placebo mechanisms to treatment effects, particularly for invasive and potentially costly treatments. On the other hand, the use of placebo controls has allowed us to better appreciate placebo effects in clinical populations and this remains an important aspect in improving the harnessing of placebo mechanisms to improve clinical care. This chapter will address issues around placebos in physical therapy and interventional trials through the lens of improving clinical trial design but also the interpretation of how placebo effects operate across physical and interventional treatments so they can be better understood and augmented in the future.

screening.rationale: Narrative review chapter explicitly focused on placebo effects, mechanisms, and trial methodology in physical and interventional therapies, matching inclusion criterion for placebo science reviews.

classification.summary: Reviews placebo mechanisms, challenges, and trial-design issues for physical therapies and interventional procedures, and discusses how to understand and harness placebo effects in clinical care.

title: The role of mindsets in placebo effects and healthcare.
abstract: Mindsets are core assumptions or beliefs about the meaning or nature of a domain or category that orient people to a particular set of expectations, attributions, and goals. In the domain of health, mindsets like "this treatment is effective," "stress is enhancing," or "my body is capable" may represent an important, yet understudied, mechanism behind placebo effects and other health outcomes. Understanding how to effectively harness mindsets in the health domain has significant implications for clinical practice and healthcare interventions, due to their potential to shape physiological, behavioral, and psychological outcomes, sometimes in profound ways. In this chapter, we introduce readers to the historical evolution and theoretical underpinnings of mindsets. We also elucidate their relevance in placebo effects, and in healthcare more broadly, by synthesizing research on established and emerging mindsets and discuss their relationship to and distinctions from more well-known psychological mechanisms, such as expectations. Additionally, we examine key challenges in research and propose avenues for future exploration, including the need to refine measurement techniques, explore contextual factors, and align terminology. In doing so, we underscore the potential of mindset-focused interventions to offer sustainable improvements to health and well-being and address some limitations of conventional placebo-based approaches.

screening.rationale: Narrative review chapter explicitly focused on mindsets as mechanisms of placebo effects and their application in healthcare, so placebo/nocebo is the main subject (review).

classification.summary: Reviewed theory and empirical evidence linking mindsets to placebo effects and broader healthcare outcomes, discussed measurement and contextual challenges, and proposed future research directions.

title: How the magnitude and precision of pain predictions shape pain experiences.
abstract: BACKGROUND: In Bayesian models including predictive processing, the magnitude and precision of pain expectancies are key determinants of perception. However, relatively few studies have directly tested whether this holds for pain, and results so far have been inconclusive. Here, we investigated expectancy effects on pain experiences and associated affective responses. METHODS: In two studies, healthy participants (n = 30 in each) received painful electrical stimuli preceded by explicit pain predictions. In study 1, the magnitude of pain predictions and administered pain intensities were varied. In study 2, the magnitude and precision of pain predictions were varied, while administered pain intensity was kept constant. Experienced pain intensity was the primary outcome in both studies. RESULTS: Pain experiences assimilated towards both under- and overpredictions of pain. In study 1, however, effects were small, if present at all, for non-painful stimuli and effects were not necessarily larger with predictions of greater magnitude. In study 2, assimilation of pain experiences appeared regardless of precision level, while no significant effects on EMG eyeblink startle responses were observed. Moreover, under- and overpredictions caused disappointment and relief, respectively, with greater disappointment upon precise than imprecise predictions. CONCLUSIONS: The influence of pain predictions on pain might be more complex than assumed in simple instantiations of current theoretical frameworks, with no systematically stronger assimilation of pain experiences to larger and more precise predictions. Since overpredictions are associated with relief, but underpredictions with disappointment, these findings underline the importance of providing correct predictions when preparing for upcoming painful procedures. SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT: Our work supports, challenges, and extends the application of Bayesian and predictive processing frameworks to the influence of pain predictions on pain. Under- and overpredictions of pain yielded assimilation of pain experiences, but assimilation was not systematically stronger with larger prediction errors or greater precision. Moreover, under- and overpredictions resulted in disappointment and relief, respectively. This research signifies the importance of establishing accurate predictions of pain in clinical practice.

screening.rationale: Experimental manipulation of explicit pain predictions (expectation magnitude and precision) tested effects on pain perception, meeting inclusion as an expectancy/placebo-related experimental study.

classification.summary: Conducted two within-subject experiments in healthy adults manipulating explicit pain predictions' magnitude and precision and found assimilation of reported pain to predictions but no EMG startle effects, with precision modulating disappointment/relief.
classification.key_finding: Pain reports assimilated toward under- and overpredictions (subjective effect), while EMG startle showed no significant effects; precise underpredictions increased disappointment.
